evidence.claim: The Blue Ridge foothills hold Ferrum College, while Fairy Stone State Park lies in Patrick County.
evidence.quote: Ferrum College's 700-acre (280 ha) campus is in the foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains near Rocky Mount, Virginia, in Franklin County.

evidence.claim: The park takes its name from the cross-shaped staurolite stones found in its vicinity.
evidence.quote: is named for the cross-shaped "fairy stones" (staurolite) commonly found in the vicinity of the park.

evidence.claim: In Ferrum, a school established in 1913 served mountain communities with primary and secondary education.
evidence.quote: The college was established in 1913 as the "Ferrum Training School" (also referred to as the "Ferrum Institute" by its board of trustees) for primary and secondary education to serve the mountain communities of rural Southwest Virginia.

evidence.claim: The railway built a cinder road from the depot to the school as the institution grew.
evidence.quote: The small school grew with the support of the railway, which constructed a cinder road from the Ferrum Depot to Ferrum Training School.

evidence.claim: Callaway has a Greek Revival church with paired front entrances; Ferrum has a college museum devoted to Blue Ridge folklore.
evidence.quote: the Flemish bond Greek Revival church, has two front entrances, shuttered windows and a pedimented front gable.

evidence.claim: Fairy Stone State Park adds a lake and structures built by the Civilian Conservation Corps, with many of those structures still in use.
evidence.quote: Some of the park's features, including its lake and many structures still in use, were built by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

evidence.claim: Ferrum has a college museum devoted to Blue Ridge folklore.
evidence.quote: The Blue Ridge Institute and Museum, designated as the State Center for Blue Ridge Folklore by the Virginia General Assembly in 1986, is on the main campus near the Blue Ridge Farm Museum.

evidence.claim: Outside Callaway, Phoebe Needles Mission School served children who could not reach public schools in Callaway, Ferrum or Rocky Mount.
evidence.quote: The school and mission church used to serve the rural and mountain children of the county who could not get to the public schools in Callaway, Ferrum, Virginia or Rocky Mount, Virginia.

evidence.claim: Its later uses continue that educational connection: the former school is now a church parish, a Center for Lifelong Learning and a summer camp operated by the Episcopal Diocese of Southwestern Virginia.
evidence.quote: The school has now become a church parish, Center for Lifelong Learning and summer camp operated by the Episcopal Diocese of Southwestern Virginia.

evidence.claim: Ferrum College began as a mountain school, with its first classes held in John Wesley Hall in the fall of 1914.
evidence.quote: opening the first section of John Wesley Hall to begin the first term of instruction in the fall of 1914.

evidence.claim: The railway built a cinder road connecting the depot and school.
evidence.quote: The small school grew with the support of the railway, which constructed a cinder road from the Ferrum Depot to Ferrum Training School.

evidence.claim: The institution moved from primary and secondary teaching into higher education, receiving accreditation as a four-year college in 1976.
evidence.quote: in 1976, Ferrum received accreditation from the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools to operate as a four-year college

evidence.claim: Regional culture also has a place on campus: the Blue Ridge Institute and Museum became the State Center for Blue Ridge Folklore in 1986.
evidence.quote: The Blue Ridge Institute and Museum, designated as the State Center for Blue Ridge Folklore by the Virginia General Assembly in 1986, is on the main campus

evidence.claim: The institute has held its annual Blue Ridge Folklife Festival since 1973 to showcase regional traditions.
evidence.quote: Since 1973, the institute has held the annual Blue Ridge Folklife Festival on the fourth Saturday in October to showcase regional traditions.

evidence.claim: Cross-shaped staurolite gives Fairy Stone State Park its name.
evidence.quote: is named for the cross-shaped "fairy stones" (staurolite) commonly found in the vicinity of the park.

evidence.claim: Junius B. Fishburn, a former owner of the Roanoke Times, donated the land in 1933.
evidence.quote: The park's land was donated in 1933 by Junius B. Fishburn, former president of the Southwest Virginia Trust Co. and former owner of the Roanoke Times.

evidence.claim: Three years later, it opened with Virginia’s first six state parks on June 15, 1936.
evidence.quote: the largest of the original Virginia six state parks that opened on June 15, 1936

evidence.claim: The Civilian Conservation Corps built the lake and many structures that remain in use.

evidence.claim: At 4,741 acres, it was the largest of those six original parks.
evidence.quote: The park is 4,741 acres (19.19 km2), making it the largest of the six original parks
